job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Adam Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Brennan and Daughters, a family tax and accounting office in Dayton. Mr Brennan took me on after my internship there. I prepare returns for about 80 households and small shops, mostly farmers' co-op members and church people. I'm in at 7:45, I wear a tie, and I'm done when the pile is done, which in tax season means 9pm. I rent a room in a house owned by a widow from my church, and my student debt is bigger than my father's whole yearly pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that I've seen a lot of talk about machines and not a lot of change. At work I'd say a good accountant needs to look a person in the eye. At church I'd say the Lord gave us hands and minds to work, and I'd say it politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried even in the quiet version, because I've no savings to speak of and the debt is huge. I did everything my parents told me: studied hard, worked summers, and now I'm told the job market's thin. There are only two accounting offices in our town and neither is hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working hard and finish my licence exams by next year, because the licence is what lets you set your own price one day. I'd pay 150 a month on the debt and eat at home. I'd keep going to church and the men's group, which is where I'd hear of any other job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady in my heart, but tight in my chest. A man can be calm about God and still be uneasy about the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your clients bring you, mostly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shoeboxes, honestly. Old men with a shoebox of receipts who don't trust a computer. They trust me because my grandfather sold them their first tractors. That's not something software can copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the office got a new program?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave it to Mr Brennan and let the others try it first. I've never used one of those chat things and I don't plan to. If the office told me to, I'd learn it, but I'd keep doing the sums by hand to check it.

I'd say a good accountant has to look a person in the **eye**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change a lot of offices, and that people should stay honest and keep working. I'd say the government shouldn't hand out money, but employers should help their own people learn. I'd keep my own counsel at church until I knew more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the bookkeeping and return preparation is the first to be taken. My job is checking numbers and filling forms, and the card says exactly that goes first. Mr Brennan would keep me out of loyalty, but I don't think he'd hire anyone after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Brennan to give me more client meetings and let me handle the tougher cases, the ones with farms and small businesses. I'd learn the new software on my own time, slowly, after others have used it. I'd cut my spending to the bone and put the Sunday collection money aside only after the debt payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit annoyed. A man should be able to learn a trade and keep it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Mr Brennan is a careful man. What would he do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Brennan would try it for a year before he trusted it. He's seen software crash and lose a month of work. He'd say clients pay for a person who answers the phone. But he's 64 and his daughter Ellen is the one who'll decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would feel it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cheryl, who does the data entry. She's 49 and has the least schooling in the office. If a program reads the receipts, she's the one who'd have nothing to do. I'd hate to see her go over a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that nobody asked us and nobody has a plan, and that the big technology firms are doing this to ordinary people. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen at church. I'd say government and the firms that cause this should do something, and then I'd feel foolish, because I don't trust government to know what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm frightened. Accounting is all numbers and rules, and that's what this thing does best. I think I'd lose my job inside two years, and I don't have any other trade. I've no savings and a debt I'll still owe at 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every extra hour I could get and ask for a pay raise before it was too late. I'd look for a trade I could learn with my hands, like electrical work or HVAC, because I've heard those will last longer. I'd talk to my pastor and ask whether the church knows of any apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid. I'd pray, I think, and then I'd still lie awake going through the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do the week you heard it was coming in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pastor Ogden first. He'd know the men in the building trades and could put in a word. Then my father, though he can't help with money. He'd say work hard and trust God, and I'd want to hear it even though I'm not sure it's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you go to for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a week to get my head straight and then I'd try to start an electrician's apprenticeship at night. It would feel like starting at 14 again. But it's honest work and the church men would respect it. I'd rather be a young man learning a trade than an old one without a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that people can prepare, and that apprenticeships should be built up in every town. I'd say it at church and at work. I'd say we should help people work, and not just pay them to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be afraid but not as much. I could finish my licence, build a client base and perhaps move into a hands-on side of business, like advising farmers. But the date still comes, and thinking work is thinking work whatever the licence says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my licence in the first year and save 200 a month. I'd learn a trade side by side, like bookkeeping for farms, which needs me to be on the land. I'd also ask Mr Brennan whether I could buy into the office in a few years, in case it turns into a person-to-person business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. I can think and not just panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go into the first two years believing it's possible. But I'd watch closely for a signal like bigger offices closing. If it came I'd switch fast, and that's why I'd want a trade in my back pocket already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think a trade would be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope so. A trade that's in people's homes and on their farms is slower to be taken. But I can't be sure; I've no way to know. It's why I'd want to learn two things, not only one.

I'd say we should help people **work** and not just pay them to wait.
think: I'd be afraid but **less**: I could finish my licence and advise farmers.
The date still comes, and thinking work is **thinking work** whatever the licence says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good thing, because there's time. I'd say don't panic, work hard, pray and prepare. I'd say it to the young men at church and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel almost fine. By 2036 I'd be 32, married perhaps, with the debt paid off and a licence. My worry is I'd put it off and wake up at 30 having done nothing. Ten years can slip by when you're busy with the next tax season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my licence and become a partner in the Brennan office if they'd have me. I'd pay 250 a month on the debt, which is the thing I want gone first. I'd also learn a second skill, maybe property management, and I'd marry and buy a small house if I can manage it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. It's the one where I think I can do what my parents hoped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what does a good life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good life is a small house, a wife, a few kids, and honest work. I don't need much. What I'd want is to be needed by people who know my name. That's why I'd stay local and not chase a big city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the young people at church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't borrow too much for a degree, learn a skill with your hands, go to the older people and ask what they know. And say your prayers, because worry takes more than it gives.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because nobody has a plan and I've no trade except one the machines do well. What would help is a real apprenticeship route, employers who put their own people first, and a bit of time to pay down the debt. I don't want a handout. I want a way to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people say the young are lazy, and then complain when we can't find jobs. We did what we were told. I'd just like the old rules to still work.

headlineQuote: We did what we were told. I'd just like the old rules to still work.
portrait: Adam is a **22-year-old** junior tax accountant in Dayton, with heavy debt, a rented room and no savings to speak of.
He's traditional, church-going and pro-work: he wants apprenticeships and employer help, not handouts.
He's never used AI tools, trusts the personal bond with farm clients and plans to learn a hands-on trade if needed.
He's anxious in most worlds, alarmed in the two-year one, and only uneasy when he has ten years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because nobody has a plan and he has only the one trade machines do well.
whatWouldHelp: A real **apprenticeship** route, employers who put their own people first, and time to pay down the debt.
